accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE National Curriculum in England, Year 5 Statistics ('solve comparison, sum and difference problems using information presented in a line graph') and Year 6 Statistics ('interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs and use these to solve problems'), with CCSS 5.G.A.2 and 6.SP.B.4. The lab's data (6 am 8 °C, 8 am 10, 10 am 16, noon 20, 2 pm 22, 4 pm 22, 6 pm 14) was recomputed for every answer: 9 am = (10+16)/2 = 13, 1 pm = 21, 3 pm = 22 on the flat part, 11 am = 18 and 5 pm = 18 are the only two crossings of 18 °C, the steepest rise is 8–10 am (+6), 2–4 pm is flat and 4–6 pm falls 8. Parameterised items 3s, a+r with a+2r shown, 10+4s and n−m are whole numbers at every corner. This lesson covers the line-graph half of the Year 6 statement; pie charts are left to their own lesson.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the graph-reading errors documented by Leinhardt, Zaslavsky & Stein (1990, 'Functions, graphs and graphing') and the NCETM/STEM Learning Year 6 statistics guidance: reading one unit per grid line on a 2 °C scale (plot feedback 'count up in 2s', challenge tags ones and tens), treating the highest part as the fastest rise (height-for-slope confusion: prediction option, segment feedback, tag high), reading a flat line as zero or missing (tags zero, gap; flat 3 pm reading), giving only one time for a repeated value (step 4 needs both crossings, prediction 'Once'), adding readings instead of interpolating (tags add, sum, 44 °C option) and joining categorical data (step 5 sort, tags join and tall).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaglinegr works on one continuous time series: the learner plots points on a 2 °C grid with instant per-point checking, drags a vertical time line to interpolate between readings, taps segments to classify their gradient, reads backwards from a horizontal 18 °C line to find two crossings, and sorts data sets into line graph or bar chart. It differs from flagbgraph and the picture/bar graph lab (categories), flaglplot (line plots of measurements), the distance–time and velocity–time labs (motion, speed from gradient) and flagline (y = mx + c). The gate reports under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found by doing it before the text confirms it: plotting four points and seeing them joined shows the shape of the day; sliding to 9 am shows a value nobody measured can be read off the line; tapping the high flat part when asked for the fastest rise is rejected with 'flat means no change'; a horizontal line at 18 °C visibly meets the graph twice; and trying to put favourite fruit on a line graph is rejected because nothing lies between categories.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'to make it look neat' / 'every graph needs a line' (the sort step shows categories must not be joined), 'only the plotted points count' for 9 am (the time line reads 13 °C), 'where the line is highest' for the fastest warming (the high flat segment is rejected), and 'once' for 18 °C (two crossings are required). Each task completion echoes the locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions, two wrong options each, each with its own message: high (highest is not fastest), start (6–8 am goes up), ones (each line is 2 °C, 10 + 6 = 16), tens (3 × 2 °C), zero (a flat line can be high), gap (both readings are 22 °C), join (only join data over time), tall (bar height does not decide), before (10 °C is the 8 am reading), add (halfway between 10 and 16 is 13), sum (difference 20 − 8) and read (20 °C is the noon reading, not the difference). In-lab plot, read and segment feedback name the specific slip too.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the learner limits; the kid paragraphs score about grade 2 and the adult text under grade 7. Canvas prompts are single lines ('Plot 8 am: 10 °C', 'Temperature at 9 am?', 'Tap where it warmed up fastest'), times are written as 9 am / 12 noon / 3 pm, and the terms steep, flat and falling are tied to the visible line.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step has one job (plot, interpolate, gradient, read backwards, choose the graph type) and every feedback line carries numbers or a reason. Item explanations show the working (3 × s, halfway rise r, 22 − 14 = 8).

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px width in light and dark, before and after Show me for every step. The grid has 2 °C lines about 10 px apart on the phone, so plotting snaps to the nearest 2-hour column and whole degree, and every plot, read and segment action also has a large button ('8 am: 10 °C', '◀ 1 hour', '8 am–10 am'). After the first pass the °C label moved off the 24 tick, the time-line label is clamped inside the plot so '6 am' no longer collides with the axis, and the 18 °C label moved to the left so it no longer covers the 5 pm crossing.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: 'Plot 10 degrees at 8 am', 'Time line on 1 hour', 'It was 13 degrees', 'From 8 am to 10 am', 'Mark this time' and 'Sort into Line graph'. The plot step's canvas aria-label lists every reading in the table, and after each move it states the live state, e.g. 'Time line at 11 am, where the line is 18 °C. Found 1 of 2 times at 18 °C.' Challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors; the canvas keeps a light card in dark mode.
